To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a marine bacterial glycolipid is able to inhibit and disrupt biofilms of pathogen bacteria and protect Artemia nauplii in a tropical aqua‐culture system.
a non‐toxicepizootic marine bacterium Staph. lentus produces a glycolipid that disrupts biofilms in aquaculture systems.

the marine biosurfactant SLSZ2 was able to inhibit the biofilm formation by V. harveyii and P. aerugenosa, disrupt mature biofilm and protect the nauplii of A. salina against V. harveii and P. aeurugenosa infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation, purification and characterization of the biofilm disrupting properties of a glycolipid produced by the marine epizootics bacterium S. lentus.
developing eco‐friendly strategies for controlling bacterial infections and reducing the use of antibiotics in aquafeed.
the discovery and characterization of a novel glycolipid BS‐SLS2, a potential biofilm inhibitor, from a marine epizoote bacterium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the biosurfactant from marine epizootics Staphylococcal species can be used to control biofilm associated infections in tropical aquaculture settings.
the glycolipoprotein biosurfactant from the epizootic Staphylococcous lentus has been identified and its mode of action has been elucidated.

the biosurfactant from S. lentus was able to disrupt biofilms of pathogen V. harvey and P. aerugionsa in an ecofriendly manner and thus, can be used to control bacterial infections in aquaculture system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a novel marine biosurfactant that can inhibit the biofilm formation by pathogenic bacteria and also disrupt the established biofilms of these bacteria.
the glycolipoprotein biosurfactant derived from marine epizootics could be used to prevent and treat infections associated with aquaculture systems.
we isolated a marine epizooic bacterium St. lentus and identified the biosurfactant it secreted.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biosurfactants are a potential alternative for the control of biofilm associated infections in aquaculture.
the biosurfactant is an effective biocontrol agent against pathogenic biofilms.
the glycolipoprotein (BS‐SlsZ2) is a potent antibiofilm agent against the two pathogenic bacteria V. harvey and P. aerugenosa, which can cause infections in shrimp farms.
